system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-08-01 21:18:00 to 2176-08-11 18:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for tachycardia, weakness, and diarrhea. He was found to have Strep gallolyticus sepsis and recurrent Clostridium difficile infection. IV and oral vancomycin were initiated, with negative follow-up blood cultures. His tachycardia resolved with volume repletion and restarting carvedilol and diltiazem. Bilateral knee pain prompted X-rays, revealing a possible lucent lesion in the right knee, raising concern for myeloma progression. His oncology team decided to switch from pomalidomide and cyclophosphamide to ixazomib outpatient. He received transfusions for pancytopenia and completed a dose of Velcade inpatient. An echocardiogram showed no endocarditis. He improved clinically, with stable vital signs and no diarrhea in hospital, and was discharged home with home IV antibiotics and close oncology follow-up.
problems: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with diabetic neuropathy, unspecified
Unspecified viral hepatitis B without hepatic coma

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  RENAL U.S.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with multiple myeloma, now with ___  // Evaluate
for hydronephrosis

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the kidneys were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  Ultrasound from ___.

FINDINGS: 

The right kidney measures 12.6 cm. The left kidney measures 12.1 cm. There is
no hydronephrosis, stones, or masses bilaterally.  Normal cortical
echogenicity and corticomedullary differentiation are seen bilaterally.

The bladder is moderately well distended and normal in appearance.

IMPRESSION: 

Normal renal ultrasound.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with multiple myeloma presenting with ___  //
Place line for temporary triple lumen plasmapheresis line with VIP. Blanch
aware.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph of ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology Fellow and Dr.
___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
___ personally supervised the trainee during the key components of the
procedure and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA:  1 mg of midazolam.  The patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  1 min 35 seconds, 129 cGy-cm2

PROCEDURE:  PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks,
benefits and alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was
obtained from the patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography
suite and placed supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was
performed per ___ protocol.  The right neck was prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.
Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the patent right internal jugular vein
was compressible and accessed using a micropuncture needle. Permanent
ultrasound images were obtained before and after intravenous access, which
confirmed vein patency. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed into the right
atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath.
The Nitinol wire was removed and a short ___ wire was advanced into the IVC.
After a serial dilatation of the percutaneous tract, a temporary pheresis
catheter with VIP port was advanced over the wire into the superior vena cava
with the tip in the cavoatrial junction. All 3 access ports were aspirated,
flushed and capped. The catheter was secured to the skin with a 0 silk suture
and sterile dressings were applied. Final spot fluoroscopic image
demonstrating good alignment of the catheter and no kinking. The patient
tolerated the procedure well without immediate complications.

FINDINGS: 

Patent right internal jugular vein. Final fluoroscopic image showing triple
lumen central venous catheter with catheter tip terminating in the distal
superior vena cava.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a temporary pheresis catheter with VIP port via the
right internal jugular venous approach. The tip of the catheter terminates in
the distal superior vena cava. The catheter is ready for use.

edema.  // please evaluate patency of LLE (rule of DVT)

on the left lower extremity veins.

COMPARISON:  US from ___

There is normal compressibility, flow, and augmentation of the left common

There is normal respiratory variation in the common femoral veins bilaterally.

No evidence of medial popliteal fossa (___) cyst.

IMPRESSION: 

No evidence of deep venous thrombosis in the left lower extremity veins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You're here because your kidney function has worsened quickly. Your creatinine was 1.1 last time, but now it's 5.0. Do you have any symptoms like fatigue or swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No swelling, and I feel okay. I’ve been eating well. I did have some rib pain, but I’m only taking Tylenol and oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, no vomiting or diarrhea. Your urine output seems normal too. Given your multiple myeloma, this kidney issue is likely due to 'cast nephropathy'—a buildup of proteins from the cancer affecting your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because of the myeloma? I’ve had rising IgA and lambda chains lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your free lambda was 942 last week—very high. That’s likely overwhelming your kidneys. We’ll start treatment right away to reduce the protein load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start chemotherapy—CyBorD: cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone. We’ll also give you plasmapheresis to filter the harmful proteins from your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Plasmapheresis? How does that work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a special line in your neck to remove your blood, filter out the abnormal proteins, and return the cleaned blood. It’s like dialysis but targets the myeloma proteins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And the chemo—same as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, CyBorD. You’ve had it before. We’re restarting it because your myeloma is progressing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a kidney ultrasound this morning. Good news—it shows no blockage or stones. Both kidneys are normal in size and appearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s physically wrong with them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No obstruction. The damage is internal, from the protein buildup. That’s why chemo and plasmapheresis are key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’ll place the pheresis line in your right neck vein. It’ll be used for plasmapheresis over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local numbing and a little sedation. You’ll feel pressure but not sharp pain. The team will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The line was placed successfully. You’ll start plasmapheresis now. We’ll do three sessions over the next few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I feel during it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people feel fine. Some get lightheaded or chilled. We’ll give fluids and monitor your blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first plasmapheresis went well. We removed a lot of abnormal protein. Your creatinine is still high at 4.8, but we expect gradual improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects from the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching for neuropathy, especially since you already have some. Bortezomib can worsen it. Let us know if your feet feel more numb or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—up to 170s. We’re increasing your carvedilol and diltiazem. We may add another medication if it doesn’t settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been stressed. Could that be why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stress can play a role, but with myeloma and kidney issues, BP control is important. We’ll get it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Second plasmapheresis done. Your creatinine is down to 3.9. That’s a good sign your kidneys are starting to recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Any update on my blood sugar? I’m on more steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sugars are higher. We’ve increased your Lantus to 46 units at night. You’ll need close monitoring after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re giving your second dose of bortezomib through the central line. How are you feeling overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but okay. My mouth feels dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you hydrated. Also, you’re still on vancomycin for C. diff. You’ve completed the intensive phase and are now on a taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll keep taking it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily at first, then every other day, then every third day. It’s to prevent another flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your third plasmapheresis is scheduled. Also, your left leg has some swelling. We did an ultrasound to check for a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to rule it out. The ultrasound showed no DVT—good news. The swelling may be from inactivity or mild fluid retention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Plasmapheresis complete. Your creatinine is now 3.1. Kidney function is steadily improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big drop!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your free lambda is coming down too. The treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is better—150s now. We added doxazosin last night, and it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dizziness when standing up. Take it at bedtime, and rise slowly. It’s to help relax your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show creatinine down to 2.6. Nephrology agrees you don’t need dialysis. You’re making good progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow, if all goes well. We’ll remove the pheresis line in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on the same chemo regimen, with vancomycin taper, insulin at 46 units, and the new doxazosin for blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin—what if my sugar drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your morning blood sugar. If it’s below 100, cut the Lantus dose in half—down to 23 units—until you see endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We removed the line—no issues. Your vitals are stable, and labs confirm continued improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m ready to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll follow up with oncology, nephrology, and endocrinology. Keep taking all meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your team or go to the ER if you have trouble urinating, severe fatigue, shortness of breath, or very low blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Keep up the good work, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Your physical exam is stable—clear lungs, normal heart, no swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have your wife pick you up. Make sure she reviews the discharge instructions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s on her way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay in touch with your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Any questions before you leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ride is here. Don’t forget your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got them. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final sign-out complete. You’re officially discharged. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re going home feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay safe and call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final chart note completed. Discharge confirmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: All set. Heading home now.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted for acute kidney injury with a creatinine rise from 1.1 to 5.0, attributed to cast nephropathy secondary to relapsed multiple myeloma. He was started on CyBorD chemotherapy and underwent three sessions of plasmapheresis, which led to improvement in renal function, with creatinine decreasing to 2.6 at discharge. He received continuous IV fluids and had a temporary pheresis line placed. His blood pressure was managed with uptitration of carvedilol and diltiazem and addition of doxazosin. Insulin was increased to 46 units of Lantus due to steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Oral vancomycin was continued on a taper for recurrent C. diff. He remained stable, avoided dialysis, and was discharged home with follow-up in oncology, nephrology, and endocrinology.
